***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tract")]

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

In [Greek mythology](/wiki/Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") the name **Andraemon** ([/ænˈdriːmən/](/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Ancient Greek](/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀνδραίμων, [romanized](/wiki/Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Andraímon*) may refer to:

* Andraemon, son of [Oxylus](/wiki/Oxylus "Oxylus") and husband of [Dryope](/wiki/Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops) "Dryope (daughter of Dryops)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)
* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](#cite_note-2)
* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](/wiki/Aetolia "Aetolia") king and husband of [Gorge](/wiki/Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)") of [Calydon](/wiki/Calydon "Calydon"). By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](/wiki/Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](/wiki/Oeneus "Oeneus")' power over [Aetolia](/wiki/Aetolia "Aetolia"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](/wiki/Amfissa "Amfissa").[[3]](#cite_note-3)
* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](/wiki/Leonteus_(mythology) "Leonteus (mythology)"). He married [Amphinome](/wiki/Amphinome "Amphinome"), a daughter of [Pelias](/wiki/Pelias "Pelias").[[4]](#cite_note-4)
* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](/wiki/Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") of [Penelope](/wiki/Penelope "Penelope") who came from [Dulichium](/wiki/Dulichium "Dulichium") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](/wiki/Odysseus "Odysseus") with the aid of [Eumaeus](/wiki/Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), [Philoetius](/wiki/Philoetius_(Odyssey) "Philoetius (Odyssey)"), and [Telemachus](/wiki/Telemachus "Telemachus").[[6]](#cite_note-6)
* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](/wiki/Codrus "Codrus"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](/wiki/Asia_Minor "Asia Minor") and drove the [Carians](/wiki/Caria "Caria") out of the city of Lebedus. His tomb was shown near [Colophon](/wiki/Colophon_(city) "Colophon (city)").[[7]](#cite_note-7) [Mimnermus](/wiki/Mimnermus "Mimnermus") related that Andraemon was a native of [Pylos](/wiki/Pylos "Pylos") and founder of Colophon.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

Similarly **Andraemonides** was a [patronymic](/wiki/Patronymic "Patronymic"), frequently used to refer to [Thoas](/wiki/Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"), son of Andraemon and [Gorge](/wiki/Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)").[[9]](#cite_note-9)

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tract")]

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

In [Greek mythology](/wiki/Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") the name **Andraemon** ([/ænˈdriːmən/](/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Ancient Greek](/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀνδραίμων, [romanized](/wiki/Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Andraímon*) may refer to:

* Andraemon, son of [Oxylus](/wiki/Oxylus "Oxylus") and husband of [Dryope](/wiki/Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops) "Dryope (daughter of Dryops)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)
* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](#cite_note-2)
* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](/wiki/Aetolia "Aetolia") king and husband of [Gorge](/wiki/Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)") of [Calydon](/wiki/Calydon "Calydon"). By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](/wiki/Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](/wiki/Oeneus "Oeneus")' power over [Aetolia](/wiki/Aetolia "Aetolia"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](/wiki/Amfissa "Amfissa").[[3]](#cite_note-3)
* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](/wiki/Leonteus_(mythology) "Leonteus (mythology)"). He married [Amphinome](/wiki/Amphinome "Amphinome"), a daughter of [Pelias](/wiki/Pelias "Pelias").[[4]](#cite_note-4)
* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](/wiki/Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") of [Penelope](/wiki/Penelope "Penelope") who came from [Dulichium](/wiki/Dulichium "Dulichium") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](/wiki/Odysseus "Odysseus") with the aid of [Eumaeus](/wiki/Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), [Philoetius](/wiki/Philoetius_(Odyssey) "Philoetius (Odyssey)"), and [Telemachus](/wiki/Telemachus "Telemachus").[[6]](#cite_note-6)
* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](/wiki/Codrus "Codrus"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](/wiki/Asia_Minor "Asia Minor") and drove the [Carians](/wiki/Caria "Caria") out of the city of Lebedus. His tomb was shown near [Colophon](/wiki/Colophon_(city) "Colophon (city)").[[7]](#cite_note-7) [Mimnermus](/wiki/Mimnermus "Mimnermus") related that Andraemon was a native of [Pylos](/wiki/Pylos "Pylos") and founder of Colophon.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

Similarly **Andraemonides** was a [patronymic](/wiki/Patronymic "Patronymic"), frequently used to refer to [Thoas](/wiki/Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"), son of Andraemon and [Gorge](/wiki/Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)").[[9]](#cite_note-9)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

In [Greek mythology](/wiki/Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") the name **Andraemon** ([/ænˈdriːmən/](/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Ancient Greek](/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀνδραίμων, [romanized](/wiki/Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Andraímon*) may refer to:

* Andraemon, son of [Oxylus](/wiki/Oxylus "Oxylus") and husband of [Dryope](/wiki/Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops) "Dryope (daughter of Dryops)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)
* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](#cite_note-2)
* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](/wiki/Aetolia "Aetolia") king and husband of [Gorge](/wiki/Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)") of [Calydon](/wiki/Calydon "Calydon"). By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](/wiki/Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](/wiki/Oeneus "Oeneus")' power over [Aetolia](/wiki/Aetolia "Aetolia"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](/wiki/Amfissa "Amfissa").[[3]](#cite_note-3)
* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](/wiki/Leonteus_(mythology) "Leonteus (mythology)"). He married [Amphinome](/wiki/Amphinome "Amphinome"), a daughter of [Pelias](/wiki/Pelias "Pelias").[[4]](#cite_note-4)
* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](/wiki/Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") of [Penelope](/wiki/Penelope "Penelope") who came from [Dulichium](/wiki/Dulichium "Dulichium") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](/wiki/Odysseus "Odysseus") with the aid of [Eumaeus](/wiki/Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), [Philoetius](/wiki/Philoetius_(Odyssey) "Philoetius (Odyssey)"), and [Telemachus](/wiki/Telemachus "Telemachus").[[6]](#cite_note-6)
* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](/wiki/Codrus "Codrus"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](/wiki/Asia_Minor "Asia Minor") and drove the [Carians](/wiki/Caria "Caria") out of the city of Lebedus. His tomb was shown near [Colophon](/wiki/Colophon_(city) "Colophon (city)").[[7]](#cite_note-7) [Mimnermus](/wiki/Mimnermus "Mimnermus") related that Andraemon was a native of [Pylos](/wiki/Pylos "Pylos") and founder of Colophon.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

Similarly **Andraemonides** was a [patronymic](/wiki/Patronymic "Patronymic"), frequently used to refer to [Thoas](/wiki/Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"), son of Andraemon and [Gorge](/wiki/Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)").[[9]](#cite_note-9)

Final antiprelatical tract by John Milton

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tract")]

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

In [Greek mythology](/wiki/Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") the name **Andraemon** ([/ænˈdriːmən/](/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Ancient Greek](/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀνδραίμων, [romanized](/wiki/Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Andraímon*) may refer to:

* Andraemon, son of [Oxylus](/wiki/Oxylus "Oxylus") and husband of [Dryope](/wiki/Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops) "Dryope (daughter of Dryops)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)
* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](#cite_note-2)
* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](/wiki/Aetolia "Aetolia") king and husband of [Gorge](/wiki/Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)") of [Calydon](/wiki/Calydon "Calydon"). By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](/wiki/Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](/wiki/Oeneus "Oeneus")' power over [Aetolia](/wiki/Aetolia "Aetolia"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](/wiki/Amfissa "Amfissa").[[3]](#cite_note-3)
* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](/wiki/Leonteus_(mythology) "Leonteus (mythology)"). He married [Amphinome](/wiki/Amphinome "Amphinome"), a daughter of [Pelias](/wiki/Pelias "Pelias").[[4]](#cite_note-4)
* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](/wiki/Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") of [Penelope](/wiki/Penelope "Penelope") who came from [Dulichium](/wiki/Dulichium "Dulichium") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](/wiki/Odysseus "Odysseus") with the aid of [Eumaeus](/wiki/Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), [Philoetius](/wiki/Philoetius_(Odyssey) "Philoetius (Odyssey)"), and [Telemachus](/wiki/Telemachus "Telemachus").[[6]](#cite_note-6)
* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](/wiki/Codrus "Codrus"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](/wiki/Asia_Minor "Asia Minor") and drove the [Carians](/wiki/Caria "Caria") out of the city of Lebedus. His tomb was shown near [Colophon](/wiki/Colophon_(city) "Colophon (city)").[[7]](#cite_note-7) [Mimnermus](/wiki/Mimnermus "Mimnermus") related that Andraemon was a native of [Pylos](/wiki/Pylos "Pylos") and founder of Colophon.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

Similarly **Andraemonides** was a [patronymic](/wiki/Patronymic "Patronymic"), frequently used to refer to [Thoas](/wiki/Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"), son of Andraemon and [Gorge](/wiki/Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)").[[9]](#cite_note-9)

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tract")]

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

In [Greek mythology](/wiki/Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") the name **Andraemon** ([/ænˈdriːmən/](/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Ancient Greek](/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀνδραίμων, [romanized](/wiki/Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Andraímon*) may refer to:

* Andraemon, son of [Oxylus](/wiki/Oxylus "Oxylus") and husband of [Dryope](/wiki/Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops) "Dryope (daughter of Dryops)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)
* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](#cite_note-2)
* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](/wiki/Aetolia "Aetolia") king and husband of [Gorge](/wiki/Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)") of [Calydon](/wiki/Calydon "Calydon"). By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](/wiki/Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](/wiki/Oeneus "Oeneus")' power over [Aetolia](/wiki/Aetolia "Aetolia"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](/wiki/Amfissa "Amfissa").[[3]](#cite_note-3)
* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](/wiki/Leonteus_(mythology) "Leonteus (mythology)"). He married [Amphinome](/wiki/Amphinome "Amphinome"), a daughter of [Pelias](/wiki/Pelias "Pelias").[[4]](#cite_note-4)
* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](/wiki/Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") of [Penelope](/wiki/Penelope "Penelope") who came from [Dulichium](/wiki/Dulichium "Dulichium") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](/wiki/Odysseus "Odysseus") with the aid of [Eumaeus](/wiki/Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), [Philoetius](/wiki/Philoetius_(Odyssey) "Philoetius (Odyssey)"), and [Telemachus](/wiki/Telemachus "Telemachus").[[6]](#cite_note-6)
* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](/wiki/Codrus "Codrus"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](/wiki/Asia_Minor "Asia Minor") and drove the [Carians](/wiki/Caria "Caria") out of the city of Lebedus. His tomb was shown near [Colophon](/wiki/Colophon_(city) "Colophon (city)").[[7]](#cite_note-7) [Mimnermus](/wiki/Mimnermus "Mimnermus") related that Andraemon was a native of [Pylos](/wiki/Pylos "Pylos") and founder of Colophon.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

Similarly **Andraemonides** was a [patronymic](/wiki/Patronymic "Patronymic"), frequently used to refer to [Thoas](/wiki/Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"), son of Andraemon and [Gorge](/wiki/Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)").[[9]](#cite_note-9)

It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts \"Milton\\'s antiprelatical tracts\") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England \"Church of England\").\\n\\nBackground\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 \"Edit section: Background\")]\\n\\nThe *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics \"Apologetics\")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts \"Milton\\'s antiprelatical tracts\"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) \"Joseph Hall (bishop)\").[[1]](#cite_note-1)\\n\\nTract\\n-----\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 \"Edit section: Tract\")]\\n\\nMilton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) \"as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded\".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) \"that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call\\'d regenerate reason\".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:\\n\\n> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)\\n\\nThemes\\n------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 \"Edit section: Themes\")]\\n\\nThe *Apology*, like many of Milton\\'s other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual\\'s character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how \"Milton\\'s self is produced in the process of writing\" and that his self is put through \"a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations\".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains \"Milton\\'s understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle \"Aristotle\")\\'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange.\"[[9]](#cite_note-9)\\n\\nSee also\\n--------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=4 \"Edit section: See also\")]\\n\\n* [Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus \"Smectymnuus\")\\n\\nNotes\\n-----\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=5 \"Edit section: Notes\")]\\n\\n1. **[^](#cite_ref-1)** Wheeler 2003 p. 273\\n2. **[^](#cite_ref-2)** Wheeler 2003 pp. 273–274\\n3. **[^](#cite_ref-3)** Milton 1953 p. 871\\n4. ^ [***a***](#cite_ref-Wheeler_p._275_4-0) [***b***](#cite_ref-Wheeler_p._275_4-1) Wheeler 2003 p. 274\\n5. **[^](#cite_ref-5)** Milton 1953 p. 874\\n6. **[^](#cite_ref-6)** Milton 1953 p. 890\\n7. **[^](#cite_ref-7)** Keeble 2003 p. 132\\n8. **[^](#cite_ref-8)** Stevens 1988 p. 268\\n9. **[^](#cite_ref-9)** Wheeler 2003 p. 275\\n\\nReferences\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=6 \"Edit section: References\")]\\n\\n* Keeble, N. (daughter of Dryops)\").[[1]](#cite_note-1)\\n* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](#cite_note-2)\\n* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](/wiki/Aetolia \"Aetolia\") king and husband of By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](/wiki/Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) \"Thoas (king of Aetoila)\"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](/wiki/Oeneus \"Oeneus\")\\' power over [Aetolia](/wiki/Aetolia \"Aetolia\"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](/wiki/Amfissa \"Amfissa\").[[3]](#cite_note-3)\\n* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](/wiki/Leonteus_(mythology) \"Leonteus (mythology)\"). He married [Amphinome](/wiki/Amphinome \"Amphinome\"), a daughter of [Pelias](/wiki/Pelias \"Pelias\").[[4]](#cite_note-4)\\n* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](/wiki/Suitors_of_Penelope \"Suitors of Penelope\") of [Penelope](/wiki/Penelope \"Penelope\") who came from [Dulichium](/wiki/Dulichium \"Dulichium\") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](/wiki/Odysseus \"Odysseus\") with the aid of [Eumaeus](/wiki/Eumaeus \"Eumaeus\"), [Philoetius](/wiki/Philoetius_(Odyssey) \"Philoetius (Odyssey)\"), and [Telemachus](/wiki/Telemachus \"Telemachus\").[[6]](#cite_note-6)\\n* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](/wiki/Codrus \"Codrus\"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](/wiki/Asia_Minor \"Asia Minor\") and drove the [Carians](/wiki/Caria \"Caria\") out of the city of Lebedus. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts \"Milton\\'s antiprelatical tracts\") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England \"Church of England\").\\n\\nBackground\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 \"Edit section: Background\")]\\n\\nThe *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics \"Apologetics\")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts \"Milton\\'s antiprelatical tracts\"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) \"Joseph Hall (bishop)\").[[1]](#cite_note-1)\\n\\nTract\\n-----\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 \"Edit section: Tract\")]\\n\\nMilton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) \"as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded\".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) \"that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call\\'d regenerate reason\".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:\\n\\n> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)\\n\\nThemes\\n------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 \"Edit section: Themes\")]\\n\\nThe *Apology*, like many of Milton\\'s other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual\\'s character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how \"Milton\\'s self is produced in the process of writing\" and that his self is put through \"a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations\".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains \"Milton\\'s understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle \"Aristotle\")\\'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange.\"[[9]](#cite_note-9)\\n\\nSee also\\n--------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=4 \"Edit section: See also\")]\\n\\n* [Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus \"Smectymnuus\")\\n\\nNotes\\n-----\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=5 \"Edit section: Notes\")]\\n\\n1. **[^](#cite_ref-1)** Wheeler 2003 p. 273\\n2. **[^](#cite_ref-2)** Wheeler 2003 pp. 273–274\\n3. **[^](#cite_ref-3)** Milton 1953 p. 871\\n4. ^ [***a***](#cite_ref-Wheeler_p._275_4-0) [***b***](#cite_ref-Wheeler_p._275_4-1) Wheeler 2003 p. 274\\n5. **[^](#cite_ref-5)** Milton 1953 p. 874\\n6. **[^](#cite_ref-6)** Milton 1953 p. 890\\n7. **[^](#cite_ref-7)** Keeble 2003 p. 132\\n8. **[^](#cite_ref-8)** Stevens 1988 p. 268\\n9. **[^](#cite_ref-9)** Wheeler 2003 p. 275\\n\\nReferences\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=6 \"Edit section: References\")]\\n\\n* Keeble, N. ***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tract")]

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

In [Greek mythology](/wiki/Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") the name **Andraemon** ([/ænˈdriːmən/](/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Ancient Greek](/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀνδραίμων, [romanized](/wiki/Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Andraímon*) may refer to:

* Andraemon, son of [Oxylus](/wiki/Oxylus "Oxylus") and husband of [Dryope](/wiki/Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops) "Dryope (daughter of Dryops)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)
* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](#cite_note-2)
* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](/wiki/Aetolia "Aetolia") king and husband of [Gorge](/wiki/Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)") of [Calydon](/wiki/Calydon "Calydon"). By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](/wiki/Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](/wiki/Oeneus "Oeneus")' power over [Aetolia](/wiki/Aetolia "Aetolia"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](/wiki/Amfissa "Amfissa").[[3]](#cite_note-3)
* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](/wiki/Leonteus_(mythology) "Leonteus (mythology)"). He married [Amphinome](/wiki/Amphinome "Amphinome"), a daughter of [Pelias](/wiki/Pelias "Pelias").[[4]](#cite_note-4)
* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](/wiki/Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") of [Penelope](/wiki/Penelope "Penelope") who came from [Dulichium](/wiki/Dulichium "Dulichium") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](/wiki/Odysseus "Odysseus") with the aid of [Eumaeus](/wiki/Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), [Philoetius](/wiki/Philoetius_(Odyssey) "Philoetius (Odyssey)"), and [Telemachus](/wiki/Telemachus "Telemachus").[[6]](#cite_note-6)
* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](/wiki/Codrus "Codrus"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](/wiki/Asia_Minor "Asia Minor") and drove the [Carians](/wiki/Caria "Caria") out of the city of Lebedus. His tomb was shown near [Colophon](/wiki/Colophon_(city) "Colophon (city)").[[7]](#cite_note-7) [Mimnermus](/wiki/Mimnermus "Mimnermus") related that Andraemon was a native of [Pylos](/wiki/Pylos "Pylos") and founder of Colophon.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

Similarly **Andraemonides** was a [patronymic](/wiki/Patronymic "Patronymic"), frequently used to refer to [Thoas](/wiki/Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"), son of Andraemon and [Gorge](/wiki/Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)").[[9]](#cite_note-9)

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tract")]

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

In [Greek mythology](/wiki/Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") the name **Andraemon** ([/ænˈdriːmən/](/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Ancient Greek](/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀνδραίμων, [romanized](/wiki/Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Andraímon*) may refer to:

* Andraemon, son of [Oxylus](/wiki/Oxylus "Oxylus") and husband of [Dryope](/wiki/Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops) "Dryope (daughter of Dryops)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)
* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](#cite_note-2)
* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](/wiki/Aetolia "Aetolia") king and husband of [Gorge](/wiki/Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)") of [Calydon](/wiki/Calydon "Calydon"). By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](/wiki/Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](/wiki/Oeneus "Oeneus")' power over [Aetolia](/wiki/Aetolia "Aetolia"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](/wiki/Amfissa "Amfissa").[[3]](#cite_note-3)
* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](/wiki/Leonteus_(mythology) "Leonteus (mythology)"). He married [Amphinome](/wiki/Amphinome "Amphinome"), a daughter of [Pelias](/wiki/Pelias "Pelias").[[4]](#cite_note-4)
* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](/wiki/Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") of [Penelope](/wiki/Penelope "Penelope") who came from [Dulichium](/wiki/Dulichium "Dulichium") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](/wiki/Odysseus "Odysseus") with the aid of [Eumaeus](/wiki/Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), [Philoetius](/wiki/Philoetius_(Odyssey) "Philoetius (Odyssey)"), and [Telemachus](/wiki/Telemachus "Telemachus").[[6]](#cite_note-6)
* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](/wiki/Codrus "Codrus"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](/wiki/Asia_Minor "Asia Minor") and drove the [Carians](/wiki/Caria "Caria") out of the city of Lebedus. His tomb was shown near [Colophon](/wiki/Colophon_(city) "Colophon (city)").[[7]](#cite_note-7) [Mimnermus](/wiki/Mimnermus "Mimnermus") related that Andraemon was a native of [Pylos](/wiki/Pylos "Pylos") and founder of Colophon.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

Similarly **Andraemonides** was a [patronymic](/wiki/Patronymic "Patronymic"), frequently used to refer to [Thoas](/wiki/Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"), son of Andraemon and [Gorge](/wiki/Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)").[[9]](#cite_note-9)

Final antiprelatical tract by John Milton

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tract")]

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

In [Greek mythology](/wiki/Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") the name **Andraemon** ([/ænˈdriːmən/](/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Ancient Greek](/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀνδραίμων, [romanized](/wiki/Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Andraímon*) may refer to:

* Andraemon, son of [Oxylus](/wiki/Oxylus "Oxylus") and husband of [Dryope](/wiki/Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops) "Dryope (daughter of Dryops)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)
* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](#cite_note-2)
* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](/wiki/Aetolia "Aetolia") king and husband of [Gorge](/wiki/Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)") of [Calydon](/wiki/Calydon "Calydon"). By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](/wiki/Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](/wiki/Oeneus "Oeneus")' power over [Aetolia](/wiki/Aetolia "Aetolia"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](/wiki/Amfissa "Amfissa").[[3]](#cite_note-3)
* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](/wiki/Leonteus_(mythology) "Leonteus (mythology)"). He married [Amphinome](/wiki/Amphinome "Amphinome"), a daughter of [Pelias](/wiki/Pelias "Pelias").[[4]](#cite_note-4)
* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](/wiki/Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") of [Penelope](/wiki/Penelope "Penelope") who came from [Dulichium](/wiki/Dulichium "Dulichium") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](/wiki/Odysseus "Odysseus") with the aid of [Eumaeus](/wiki/Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), [Philoetius](/wiki/Philoetius_(Odyssey) "Philoetius (Odyssey)"), and [Telemachus](/wiki/Telemachus "Telemachus").[[6]](#cite_note-6)
* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](/wiki/Codrus "Codrus"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](/wiki/Asia_Minor "Asia Minor") and drove the [Carians](/wiki/Caria "Caria") out of the city of Lebedus. His tomb was shown near [Colophon](/wiki/Colophon_(city) "Colophon (city)").[[7]](#cite_note-7) [Mimnermus](/wiki/Mimnermus "Mimnermus") related that Andraemon was a native of [Pylos](/wiki/Pylos "Pylos") and founder of Colophon.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

Similarly **Andraemonides** was a [patronymic](/wiki/Patronymic "Patronymic"), frequently used to refer to [Thoas](/wiki/Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"), son of Andraemon and [Gorge](/wiki/Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)").[[9]](#cite_note-9)

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tract")]

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

In [Greek mythology](/wiki/Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") the name **Andraemon** ([/ænˈdriːmən/](/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Ancient Greek](/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀνδραίμων, [romanized](/wiki/Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Andraímon*) may refer to:

* Andraemon, son of [Oxylus](/wiki/Oxylus "Oxylus") and husband of [Dryope](/wiki/Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops) "Dryope (daughter of Dryops)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)
* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](#cite_note-2)
* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](/wiki/Aetolia "Aetolia") king and husband of [Gorge](/wiki/Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)") of [Calydon](/wiki/Calydon "Calydon"). By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](/wiki/Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](/wiki/Oeneus "Oeneus")' power over [Aetolia](/wiki/Aetolia "Aetolia"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](/wiki/Amfissa "Amfissa").[[3]](#cite_note-3)
* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](/wiki/Leonteus_(mythology) "Leonteus (mythology)"). He married [Amphinome](/wiki/Amphinome "Amphinome"), a daughter of [Pelias](/wiki/Pelias "Pelias").[[4]](#cite_note-4)
* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](/wiki/Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") of [Penelope](/wiki/Penelope "Penelope") who came from [Dulichium](/wiki/Dulichium "Dulichium") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](/wiki/Odysseus "Odysseus") with the aid of [Eumaeus](/wiki/Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), [Philoetius](/wiki/Philoetius_(Odyssey) "Philoetius (Odyssey)"), and [Telemachus](/wiki/Telemachus "Telemachus").[[6]](#cite_note-6)
* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](/wiki/Codrus "Codrus"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](/wiki/Asia_Minor "Asia Minor") and drove the [Carians](/wiki/Caria "Caria") out of the city of Lebedus. His tomb was shown near [Colophon](/wiki/Colophon_(city) "Colophon (city)").[[7]](#cite_note-7) [Mimnermus](/wiki/Mimnermus "Mimnermus") related that Andraemon was a native of [Pylos](/wiki/Pylos "Pylos") and founder of Colophon.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

Similarly **Andraemonides** was a [patronymic](/wiki/Patronymic "Patronymic"), frequently used to refer to [Thoas](/wiki/Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"), son of Andraemon and [Gorge](/wiki/Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)").[[9]](#cite_note-9)

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tract")]

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

In [Greek mythology](/wiki/Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") the name **Andraemon** ([/ænˈdriːmən/](/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Ancient Greek](/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀνδραίμων, [romanized](/wiki/Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Andraímon*) may refer to:

* Andraemon, son of [Oxylus](/wiki/Oxylus "Oxylus") and husband of [Dryope](/wiki/Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops) "Dryope (daughter of Dryops)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)
* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](#cite_note-2)
* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](/wiki/Aetolia "Aetolia") king and husband of [Gorge](/wiki/Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)") of [Calydon](/wiki/Calydon "Calydon"). By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](/wiki/Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](/wiki/Oeneus "Oeneus")' power over [Aetolia](/wiki/Aetolia "Aetolia"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](/wiki/Amfissa "Amfissa").[[3]](#cite_note-3)
* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](/wiki/Leonteus_(mythology) "Leonteus (mythology)"). He married [Amphinome](/wiki/Amphinome "Amphinome"), a daughter of [Pelias](/wiki/Pelias "Pelias").[[4]](#cite_note-4)
* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](/wiki/Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") of [Penelope](/wiki/Penelope "Penelope") who came from [Dulichium](/wiki/Dulichium "Dulichium") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](/wiki/Odysseus "Odysseus") with the aid of [Eumaeus](/wiki/Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), [Philoetius](/wiki/Philoetius_(Odyssey) "Philoetius (Odyssey)"), and [Telemachus](/wiki/Telemachus "Telemachus").[[6]](#cite_note-6)
* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](/wiki/Codrus "Codrus"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](/wiki/Asia_Minor "Asia Minor") and drove the [Carians](/wiki/Caria "Caria") out of the city of Lebedus. His tomb was shown near [Colophon](/wiki/Colophon_(city) "Colophon (city)").[[7]](#cite_note-7) [Mimnermus](/wiki/Mimnermus "Mimnermus") related that Andraemon was a native of [Pylos](/wiki/Pylos "Pylos") and founder of Colophon.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

Similarly **Andraemonides** was a [patronymic](/wiki/Patronymic "Patronymic"), frequently used to refer to [Thoas](/wiki/Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"), son of Andraemon and [Gorge](/wiki/Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)").[[9]](#cite_note-9)

Final antiprelatical tract by John Milton

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tract")]

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

In [Greek mythology](/wiki/Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") the name **Andraemon** ([/ænˈdriːmən/](/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Ancient Greek](/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀνδραίμων, [romanized](/wiki/Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Andraímon*) may refer to:

* Andraemon, son of [Oxylus](/wiki/Oxylus "Oxylus") and husband of [Dryope](/wiki/Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops) "Dryope (daughter of Dryops)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)
* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](#cite_note-2)
* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](/wiki/Aetolia "Aetolia") king and husband of [Gorge](/wiki/Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)") of [Calydon](/wiki/Calydon "Calydon"). By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](/wiki/Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](/wiki/Oeneus "Oeneus")' power over [Aetolia](/wiki/Aetolia "Aetolia"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](/wiki/Amfissa "Amfissa").[[3]](#cite_note-3)
* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](/wiki/Leonteus_(mythology) "Leonteus (mythology)"). He married [Amphinome](/wiki/Amphinome "Amphinome"), a daughter of [Pelias](/wiki/Pelias "Pelias").[[4]](#cite_note-4)
* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](/wiki/Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") of [Penelope](/wiki/Penelope "Penelope") who came from [Dulichium](/wiki/Dulichium "Dulichium") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](/wiki/Odysseus "Odysseus") with the aid of [Eumaeus](/wiki/Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), [Philoetius](/wiki/Philoetius_(Odyssey) "Philoetius (Odyssey)"), and [Telemachus](/wiki/Telemachus "Telemachus").[[6]](#cite_note-6)
* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](/wiki/Codrus "Codrus"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](/wiki/Asia_Minor "Asia Minor") and drove the [Carians](/wiki/Caria "Caria") out of the city of Lebedus. His tomb was shown near [Colophon](/wiki/Colophon_(city) "Colophon (city)").[[7]](#cite_note-7) [Mimnermus](/wiki/Mimnermus "Mimnermus") related that Andraemon was a native of [Pylos](/wiki/Pylos "Pylos") and founder of Colophon.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

Similarly **Andraemonides** was a [patronymic](/wiki/Patronymic "Patronymic"), frequently used to refer to [Thoas](/wiki/Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"), son of Andraemon and [Gorge](/wiki/Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)").[[9]](#cite_note-9)

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tract")]

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

His tomb was shown near [Colophon](/wiki/Colophon_(city) \"Colophon (city)\").[[7]](#cite_note-7) [Mimnermus](/wiki/Mimnermus \"Mimnermus\") related that Andraemon was a native of [Pylos](/wiki/Pylos \"Pylos\") and founder of Colophon.[[8]](#cite_note-8)\\n\\nSimilarly **Andraemonides** was a [patronymic](/wiki/Patronymic \"Patronymic\"), frequently used to refer to [Thoas](/wiki/Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) \"Thoas (king of Aetoila)\"), son of Andraemon and [Gorge](/wiki/Gorge_(mythology) \"Gorge (mythology)\").[[9]](#cite_note-9)\\n\\nNotes\\n-----\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Andraemon&action=edit&section=1 \"Edit section: Notes\")]\\n\\n* ![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/Parthenon_from_west.jpg/40px-Parthenon_from_west.jpg)[Ancient Greece portal](/wiki/Portal:Ancient_Greece \"Portal:Ancient Greece\")\\n* ![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e9/Draig.svg/40px-Draig.svg.png)[Myths portal](/wiki/Portal:Myths \"Portal:Myths\")\\n\\n1. **[^](#cite_ref-1)** [Ovid](/wiki/Ovid \"Ovid\"), *[Metamorphoses](/wiki/Metamorphoses \"Metamorphoses\")* 9.333; It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts \"Milton\\'s antiprelatical tracts\") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England \"Church of England\").\\n\\nBackground\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 \"Edit section: Background\")]\\n\\nThe *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics \"Apologetics\")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts \"Milton\\'s antiprelatical tracts\"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) \"Joseph Hall (bishop)\").[[1]](#cite_note-1)\\n\\nTract\\n-----\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 \"Edit section: Tract\")]\\n\\nMilton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) \"as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded\".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) \"that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call\\'d regenerate reason\".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:\\n\\n> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)\\n\\nThemes\\n------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 \"Edit section: Themes\")]\\n\\nThe *Apology*, like many of Milton\\'s other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual\\'s character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how \"Milton\\'s self is produced in the process of writing\" and that his self is put through \"a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations\".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains \"Milton\\'s understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle \"Aristotle\")\\'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange.\"[[9]](#cite_note-9)\\n\\nSee also\\n--------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=4 \"Edit section: See also\")]\\n\\n* [Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus \"Smectymnuus\")\\n\\nNotes\\n-----\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=5 \"Edit section: Notes\")]\\n\\n1. **[^](#cite_ref-1)** Wheeler 2003 p. 273\\n2. **[^](#cite_ref-2)** Wheeler 2003 pp. 273–274\\n3. **[^](#cite_ref-3)** Milton 1953 p. 871\\n4. ^ [***a***](#cite_ref-Wheeler_p._275_4-0) [***b***](#cite_ref-Wheeler_p._275_4-1) Wheeler 2003 p. 274\\n5. **[^](#cite_ref-5)** Milton 1953 p. 874\\n6. **[^](#cite_ref-6)** Milton 1953 p. 890\\n7. **[^](#cite_ref-7)** Keeble 2003 p. 132\\n8. **[^](#cite_ref-8)** Stevens 1988 p. 268\\n9. **[^](#cite_ref-9)** Wheeler 2003 p. 275\\n\\nReferences\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=6 \"Edit section: References\")]\\n\\n* Keeble, N. (daughter of Dryops)\").[[1]](#cite_note-1)\\n* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](#cite_note-2)\\n* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](/wiki/Aetolia \"Aetolia\") king and husband of By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](/wiki/Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) \"Thoas (king of Aetoila)\"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](/wiki/Oeneus \"Oeneus\")\\' power over [Aetolia](/wiki/Aetolia \"Aetolia\"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](/wiki/Amfissa \"Amfissa\").[[3]](#cite_note-3)\\n* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](/wiki/Leonteus_(mythology) \"Leonteus (mythology)\"). He married [Amphinome](/wiki/Amphinome \"Amphinome\"), a daughter of [Pelias](/wiki/Pelias \"Pelias\").[[4]](#cite_note-4)\\n* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](/wiki/Suitors_of_Penelope \"Suitors of Penelope\") of [Penelope](/wiki/Penelope \"Penelope\") who came from [Dulichium](/wiki/Dulichium \"Dulichium\") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](/wiki/Odysseus \"Odysseus\") with the aid of [Eumaeus](/wiki/Eumaeus \"Eumaeus\"), [Philoetius](/wiki/Philoetius_(Odyssey) \"Philoetius (Odyssey)\"), and [Telemachus](/wiki/Telemachus \"Telemachus\").[[6]](#cite_note-6)\\n* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](/wiki/Codrus \"Codrus\"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](/wiki/Asia_Minor \"Asia Minor\") and drove the [Carians](/wiki/Caria \"Caria\") out of the city of Lebedus.
